units.title: How a Bill Becomes Law
units.blurb: Follow an idea from a student's notebook all the way to the President's desk.

cards.heading: Anyone can have the idea
cards.body: Laws start as ideas, and those ideas can come from anyone: a student, a business owner, a group of neighbors, or a member of Congress. Citizens can't introduce bills themselves, but they can ask their representatives to.

cards.heading: Only Congress introduces bills
cards.body: Only a Member of Congress can formally introduce a bill. In the House it gets the label H.R. and a number. In the Senate it is S. and a number. The Member who introduces it is the sponsor.

cards.heading: Committees do the heavy lifting
cards.body: After introduction, a bill is sent to a committee that focuses on that subject, like Education or Agriculture. Committees hold hearings, hear from experts, and 'mark up' (edit) the text. Most bills never make it out of committee, and that is where the majority of bills quietly end.

cards.heading: Why committees exist
cards.body: Thousands of bills are introduced every Congress. Committees let small groups of Members become experts on a topic so the full chamber doesn't have to study every single bill in detail.

quiz.prompt: Who can formally introduce a bill in Congress?
quiz.explanation: Only Members of Congress can introduce bills. Citizens can ask their representatives to sponsor one.

quiz.prompt: What does 'H.R.' in front of a bill number mean?
choices: The bill started in the House of Representatives
The bill is a Highest Ranking bill
The bill was written by the Human Resources committee
The bill is a hearing request
quiz.explanation: H.R. bills are introduced in the House of Representatives. Senate bills start with S.

quiz.prompt: What happens to most bills after they are sent to committee?
choices: They become law within a week
They are signed by the President
They never advance out of committee
They go straight to the Supreme Court
quiz.explanation: The large majority of introduced bills never make it out of committee.

cards.heading: The floor vote
cards.body: If a committee approves a bill, it goes to the full chamber for debate and a vote. In each chamber a simple majority is needed to pass it.

cards.heading: Two chambers, one text
cards.body: The House and Senate must pass the exact same version of a bill. If their versions differ, the chambers negotiate to combine them, and both then vote on the final text.

cards.heading: The President's choice
cards.body: Once a bill passes both chambers it goes to the President. The President can sign it into law or veto it (send it back with objections).

cards.heading: Overriding a veto
cards.body: Congress can override a veto if two-thirds of the House AND two-thirds of the Senate vote to do so. Overrides are rare because that is a very high bar.

quiz.prompt: How many chambers of Congress must pass the same bill text?
quiz.explanation: Both the House and the Senate must pass identical text before a bill goes to the President.

quiz.prompt: What can the President do with a bill that passes Congress?
quiz.explanation: The President can sign the bill or veto it.

quiz.prompt: What is needed to override a veto?
choices: A simple majority of the House
Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate
A vote of the state governors
quiz.explanation: A veto override requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

action.title: Ask a representative about a bill
action.detail: Pick an issue you care about and tell your Member of Congress. Real constituent messages get counted.

units.title: Three Branches
units.blurb: Why power is split three ways, and how each branch keeps the others honest.

cards.heading: Legislative: makes the laws
cards.body: Article I of the Constitution creates Congress: the House of Representatives and the Senate. Congress writes laws, sets the federal budget, and can declare war.

cards.heading: Executive: carries out the laws
cards.body: Article II creates the presidency. The President leads the executive branch, which includes the Vice President, the Cabinet, and federal agencies that carry out the laws.

cards.heading: Judicial: interprets the laws
cards.body: Article III creates the Supreme Court and lets Congress create lower federal courts. Judges decide cases and what the law and the Constitution mean.

cards.heading: Why split power?
cards.body: The Founders had lived under a king and worried about too much power in one place. Dividing government into three branches makes it harder for any one person or group to control everything.

quiz.prompt: Which branch writes federal laws?
quiz.explanation: Congress, the legislative branch, writes federal laws.

quiz.prompt: The Supreme Court belongs to which branch?
quiz.explanation: The Supreme Court is the head of the judicial branch, created by Article III.

quiz.prompt: Why did the Founders divide power among three branches?
choices: To prevent any one person or group from having too much power
quiz.explanation: Separation of powers was designed to prevent concentration of power.

sources.title: USA.gov: Branches of the U.S. Government

cards.heading: Each branch can check the others
cards.body: Separate powers are not enough on their own, so each branch also has tools to limit the others. This system is called checks and balances.

cards.heading: Examples in action
cards.body: The President can veto laws passed by Congress. Congress can override a veto, approve or reject Cabinet and judicial nominees (the Senate), and impeach officials. Courts can rule that a law or action is unconstitutional.

cards.heading: Judicial review
cards.body: In the 1803 case Marbury v. Madison, the Supreme Court established judicial review: the power to decide whether laws and government actions violate the Constitution.

cards.heading: Not a perfect machine
cards.body: Checks and balances only work when people use them and pay attention. That is one reason an informed public matters.

quiz.prompt: Which is an example of the executive branch checking Congress?
quiz.explanation: The President's veto is a check on Congress.

quiz.prompt: What did Marbury v. Madison (1803) establish?
choices: The power of the Electoral College
quiz.explanation: The case established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review.

quiz.prompt: Which body confirms Supreme Court nominees?
quiz.explanation: The Senate provides 'advice and consent' on judicial nominees.

sources.title: USA.gov: Branches of the U.S. Government

units.title: Federal, State & Local
units.blurb: Who really decides what, from the White House to your school board.

cards.heading: Federalism
cards.body: The U.S. shares power between a national government and state governments. This is called federalism. The 10th Amendment says powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or the people.

cards.heading: Federal focus
cards.body: The federal government handles things like national defense, printing currency, regulating trade between states, and immigration and citizenship.

cards.heading: State focus
cards.body: States run their own courts and most elections, issue driver's licenses, set many education and health policies, and can have their own criminal laws.

cards.heading: Local focus
cards.body: Cities, counties and school districts handle things closest to daily life: local police and fire, public schools, zoning, parks, trash and water, and local roads.

cards.heading: When laws conflict
cards.body: The Constitution's Supremacy Clause says federal law wins when it truly conflicts with state law, as long as the federal law is constitutional.

quiz.prompt: Which level of government usually runs your local public school district?
quiz.explanation: Local school districts run schools day to day, with state rules and funding involved.

quiz.prompt: Which is mainly a federal responsibility?
quiz.explanation: Currency is federal. Driver's licenses are state, and trash and zoning are local.

quiz.prompt: What does the Supremacy Clause say?
choices: Federal law wins over conflicting state law
The President can overrule the courts
quiz.explanation: Valid federal law takes priority over conflicting state law.

cards.heading: The government closest to you
cards.body: City councils, county boards and school boards decide things you feel every day: school schedules, bike lanes, park hours, library funding, and how your town spends its budget.

cards.heading: Meetings are open
cards.body: Most local government meetings are open to the public, and many are streamed online. Agendas are usually posted in advance, so you can see what will be discussed.

cards.heading: Public comment
cards.body: Many boards set aside time for public comment, where residents can speak for a few minutes. A short, specific, respectful comment can genuinely influence a decision.

cards.heading: Small numbers, big impact
cards.body: Local votes and meetings often involve far fewer people than federal ones, so one informed person showing up can have an outsized effect.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is decided by local government?
quiz.explanation: Parks are typically a city or county responsibility.

quiz.prompt: What is 'public comment'?
choices: A time when residents can address the board
quiz.explanation: Public comment lets residents speak to officials during a meeting.

quiz.prompt: Where can you usually find what a city council will discuss?
quiz.explanation: Agendas are normally posted ahead of meetings.

action.title: Watch or attend a local meeting
action.detail: Look up your city council or school board schedule and watch one meeting (many are streamed). Note one decision they made.

units.title: Elections & Voting
units.blurb: Registration, primaries, the Electoral College, and how your vote fits in.

cards.heading: The voting age
cards.body: The 26th Amendment (ratified in 1971) set the national voting age at 18. Citizens who are 18 or older on Election Day can generally vote if they meet their state's rules.

cards.heading: Registration
cards.body: In almost every state you must register before you can vote. Rules and deadlines vary by state, and many states let you check or complete registration online. Many states also let you pre-register before you turn 18.

cards.heading: Primary vs. general
cards.body: Primary elections decide who will represent each party on the ballot. The general election is when voters choose between the candidates who advanced.

cards.heading: States run elections
cards.body: Elections are run mostly by states and counties, which is why voting deadlines, ID rules, and voting by mail differ depending on where you live.

quiz.prompt: Which amendment set the voting age at 18?
quiz.explanation: The 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to 18 in 1971.

quiz.prompt: What is a primary election?
choices: An election to choose party candidates for the ballot
An election only for the President
quiz.explanation: Primaries decide which candidates represent each party in the general election.

quiz.prompt: Who mostly runs elections in the U.S.?
quiz.explanation: States and local election offices run elections, so rules vary by location.

action.title: Check your voter registration
action.detail: Use vote.gov to find your state's registration rules, check your status, or find out how to pre-register.

cards.heading: How presidents are chosen
cards.body: Americans don't vote for President directly. Instead, voters in each state choose electors who then cast the electoral votes.

cards.heading: The numbers
cards.body: There are 538 electors in total, and a candidate needs 270 to win. Each state's number equals its House seats plus its two Senate seats. Washington, D.C. has 3 electors.

cards.heading: Winner-take-all
cards.body: In most states, the candidate who wins the state's popular vote gets all its electoral votes. Maine and Nebraska divide theirs in a different way.

cards.heading: Why it matters
cards.body: Because of this system, a candidate can win the presidency without winning the national popular vote, which has happened in a few elections. People disagree about whether the system should change, and understanding how it works helps you join that debate.

quiz.prompt: How many electoral votes does a candidate need to win the presidency?
quiz.explanation: There are 538 electoral votes, and a majority (270) is needed.

quiz.prompt: A state's number of electors equals...
choices: Its House seats plus 2 Senate seats
quiz.explanation: Electors = number of Representatives + 2 Senators.

quiz.prompt: In most states, electoral votes are awarded...
quiz.explanation: Most states use winner-take-all. Maine and Nebraska split theirs.

units.title: Your Rights
units.blurb: The Bill of Rights, and what it means for students today.

cards.heading: Ten amendments
cards.body: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791. They protect individual liberties and limit what government can do.

cards.heading: The First Amendment
cards.body: It protects five freedoms: religion, speech, press, assembly, and the right to petition the government for a redress of grievances (that means asking it to fix a problem).

cards.heading: Fair treatment
cards.body: The 4th Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. The 5th and 6th protect due process, the right to a fair trial, and the right to a lawyer in criminal cases.

cards.heading: Rights have limits
cards.body: No right is absolute. Courts balance individual rights against other important interests, which is why many famous Supreme Court cases are about where the line is.

quiz.prompt: How many amendments make up the Bill of Rights?
quiz.explanation: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT one of the five First Amendment freedoms?
quiz.explanation: The right to bear arms is in the Second Amendment.

quiz.prompt: The right to petition the government means...
choices: The right to ask it to address a problem
The right to a trial by jury
The right to vote in every election
quiz.explanation: Petitioning is asking the government to address grievances, for example by contacting your representatives.

sources.title: National Archives: The Bill of Rights

cards.heading: Students have rights too
cards.body: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), students wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War and were suspended. The Supreme Court ruled that students do not 'shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.'

cards.heading: But schools can set limits
cards.body: Schools can restrict speech that substantially disrupts learning or interferes with others' rights. Later cases also gave schools some authority over school-sponsored activities like student newspapers.

cards.heading: Know the rules
cards.body: Student handbooks and state laws matter. If you think a rule goes too far, you can raise it respectfully with your school board, which is an example of using your right to petition.

cards.heading: Speaking up, responsibly
cards.body: Using your rights responsibly means being informed, respectful, and ready to listen to people who disagree with you.

quiz.prompt: What did Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) decide?
choices: Students have no free speech rights at school
Students keep free speech rights at school, within limits
quiz.explanation: The Court said students keep their rights, though schools can limit substantially disruptive speech.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is an example of petitioning your government?
choices: Speaking at a school board meeting
quiz.explanation: Speaking at a public meeting is a direct way to petition.

quiz.prompt: Can schools ever limit student speech?
choices: Yes, if it substantially disrupts learning
quiz.explanation: Speech that substantially disrupts school activities can be limited.

action.title: Teach one thing to a friend
action.detail: Pick one fact you learned and explain it to a friend or family member. Teaching is the best way to remember.

units.title: Stay Informed
units.blurb: Being an aware citizen starts with knowing what's true. Learn to check sources like a pro.

cards.heading: News, opinion, and ads
cards.body: Not everything that looks like news is news. News reports try to describe what happened. Opinion pieces argue for a point of view. Sponsored content is advertising made to look like an article. Knowing which one you're reading changes how much weight to give it.

cards.heading: Headlines aren't the whole story
cards.body: Headlines are short, and they are often written to grab attention. Read past the headline before you decide what you think or share it. A story's details can be very different from what its headline suggests.

cards.heading: Check who's behind it
cards.body: Before trusting a claim, ask: Who made this? What do they want? What is their evidence? Can I find the same information from other reliable sources? A quick search about the source itself often tells you a lot.

cards.heading: Lateral reading
cards.body: Professional fact-checkers don't stay on one page. They open new tabs to see what other sources say about the site or claim. This is called lateral reading, and studies of fact-checkers suggest it works better than only looking at the page itself.

cards.heading: Slow down when you feel strong emotion
cards.body: Posts designed to make you angry or scared spread fastest. If something makes you feel a strong reaction, that's a good moment to pause and check it before you share it.

quiz.prompt: What is lateral reading?
choices: Opening other tabs to check what others say about a source or claim
quiz.explanation: Lateral reading means leaving the page to see what other sources say about it.

quiz.prompt: Which is designed to persuade you toward a point of view?
quiz.explanation: Opinion pieces argue for a position, while news reports aim to describe events.

quiz.prompt: What is a good habit before sharing a shocking post?
choices: Pause and check it against other reliable sources
Only check the number of likes
quiz.explanation: Slowing down and verifying stops false information from spreading.

sources.title: Stanford Digital Inquiry Group: Civic Online Reasoning

action.title: Fact-check one thing
action.detail: Pick a claim you saw online this week. Open new tabs and find two other sources that report it. Tell a friend what you found.

cards.heading: Primary sources
cards.body: A primary source is the original: the actual text of a bill, a court's written opinion, a transcript, or official data. A secondary source, like a news article, tells you about it. Whenever you can, check the primary source yourself.

cards.heading: Read the bill itself
cards.body: Congress.gov is the official site for U.S. legislative information. You can search for a bill, read its text, see who sponsored it, and follow where it is in the process. Bill summaries and news stories can miss details that the text itself contains.

cards.heading: Fact vs. opinion
cards.body: A fact can be checked and shown to be true or false, like how a member voted. An opinion is a judgment, like whether that vote was good. Both matter in politics, and the skill is telling them apart.

cards.heading: Look for several perspectives
cards.body: On a hard issue, reasonable people often disagree about priorities, not just facts. Reading a few sources with different viewpoints helps you understand the debate, and makes your own opinion stronger.

cards.heading: Being aware means staying curious
cards.body: No one can know everything. Awareness is a habit: check where information comes from, keep learning, and be willing to change your mind when the evidence changes.

quiz.prompt: Which is a primary source about a bill?
quiz.explanation: The official text is the original, primary source.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is a fact that can be checked?
choices: That bill is a terrible idea
The Senate voted on the bill on a certain date
quiz.explanation: Whether a vote happened on a date can be verified. The others are opinions.

quiz.prompt: Which official site lets you read bill text and track its status?
quiz.explanation: Congress.gov is the official source for federal legislative information.

units.title: Get Involved
units.blurb: You don't have to wait until you're 18 to make a difference. Here's how to start.

cards.heading: They work for you
cards.body: Members of Congress represent the people in their state or district. Hearing from constituents helps them understand what people care about. You can contact them even if you can't vote yet.

cards.heading: Ways to reach them
cards.body: Most offices accept messages through a contact form on their website, and many take phone calls. Some also take letters. Members hold events like town halls where you can ask questions in person.

cards.heading: Make it count
cards.body: Be brief and respectful. Say who you are (a student who lives in their district), name the specific issue or bill, say why it matters to you, and say what you would like them to do. Personal stories are powerful.

cards.heading: Find the right person
cards.body: Your Representative in the House serves your district, and you have two Senators for your whole state. The Act tab in this app can find all three from your ZIP code.

cards.heading: Follow up
cards.body: A response might be a form letter or a note from a staff member, and that's normal. Keep learning about the issue and stay in touch. Consistent, polite voices are hard to ignore.

quiz.prompt: Who represents you in the U.S. Senate?
choices: It depends on your ZIP code
quiz.explanation: Every state has two U.S. Senators, so everyone in a state shares the same two.

quiz.prompt: Which makes a message to a representative more effective?
choices: Being specific about the issue and what you want
quiz.explanation: Clear, respectful, specific messages from constituents work best.

quiz.prompt: Can you contact your representative if you're under 18?
choices: Yes, anyone can share their views
quiz.explanation: You can share your views with your representatives at any age.

action.title: Write to a representative
action.detail: Use the Act tab to find your representatives and draft a short, respectful message about an issue you care about.

cards.heading: Civic life is more than voting
cards.body: Voting matters, and so does everything in between elections: attending meetings, volunteering, helping others register, and speaking up when you see a problem.

cards.heading: Work at the polls
cards.body: Elections rely on poll workers to run voting sites. Rules about who can serve are set by each state, and some states let students work at the polls before they turn 18. Check your state's or county's election office for details.

cards.heading: Get involved locally
cards.body: Many towns have youth councils, student advisory boards, and volunteer groups. Attending a city council or school board meeting is a great first step, and many meetings have a time for public comment.

cards.heading: Help others take part
cards.body: You can help friends and family check their voter registration, find their polling place, and understand what is on the ballot. Sharing accurate information is a real form of civic service.

cards.heading: Start small, keep going
cards.body: Civic action can begin with one email, one meeting, or one conversation. The habit of paying attention and taking part adds up over a lifetime.

quiz.prompt: Who decides who can be a poll worker?
choices: Each state sets its own rules
quiz.explanation: Poll worker rules vary by state, and some allow high school students to help.

quiz.prompt: Which is a good first step for local involvement?
choices: Attend a city council or school board meeting
quiz.explanation: Local meetings are open to the public and a great way to start.

quiz.prompt: Which of these counts as civic action?
choices: Helping a friend check their voter registration
quiz.explanation: Helping others take part in elections is a real civic contribution.

sources.title: U.S. Election Assistance Commission: Become a Poll Worker

action.title: Help someone else take part
action.detail: Ask a friend or family member if they've checked their voter registration, and share vote.gov with them.

Involving support from members of both major political parties.
Money that Congress sets aside for a specific purpose.
